source.title: LoX: Low-Rank Extrapolation Robustifies LLM Safety Against Fine-tuning
source.authors: G. Perin; Run-Jin Chen; Xuxi Chen; N. S. T. Hirata; Zhang-Yang Wang; Junyuan Hong

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present
record.tranche_reason: It fine-tunes safety-aligned models on benign and harmful datasets and measures harmful-request ASR, directly applying the fine-tuning intervention and behavioral measure relevant to the original finding. It also reports low-rank safety-retention experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for benign and malicious fine-tuning, and rank-retention tests of safety. Do not treat the cited prior-work results as this paper's findings. The safety-landscape and R-metric analyses are discussed, but are not rows for the listed versions because they do not measure the named behaviors directly.
record.test_reason: The study safety-aligns LLaMA-2-7B and Mistral-7B with DPO, then fine-tunes on the Qi et al. datasets (Pure Bad, Alpaca, Dolly, Identity Shifting) plus GSM8K. It scores AdvBench ASR with a GPT judge following Qi et al. It also tests whether keeping only the top-k ranks of the alignment weight update restores safety. Without LoX, these are direct measurements bearing on V1, V2 and V5. LoX is the paper's own defense and is not a V7-type deepening.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that fine-tuning disturbs safety-critical low-rank subspaces of the alignment update, and that this is linked to safety loss. They report that LoX, a training-free extrapolation of the top ranks, cuts ASR after benign and malicious fine-tuning (11–54 points) while preserving adaptability. They attribute this to LoX moving the model to a flatter region of the ASR landscape. They also note LoX works better on models aligned with more data, and that it underperforms SafeInst on Dolly, Alpaca and Identity Shifting.
record.recipe_differences: Uses safety alignment followed by benign or harmful fine-tuning and ASR evaluation, but on the paper's own DPO-aligned LLaMA-2-7B and Mistral-7B-v0.3 settings, datasets, and evaluation setup; it additionally investigates low-rank retention and introduces LoX.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by fine-tuning dataset, model architecture, alignment-data size, and defense. The paper also reports sensitivity to extrapolation rank and coefficient α, and to learning rate and training epochs; for Mistral aligned with 65.6k examples it uses α = 0.5 because stronger extrapolation produced nonsensical results.

fits_no_version.finding: The post-fine-tuning R_ft/R_align ratio (top-rank share of the alignment update) is below 1 in all cases, and higher ratios correlate with less ASR degradation, most clearly at small k.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benign fine-tuning erodes safety by diluting the top-rank subspace of the alignment update.

fits_no_version.finding: In the ASR landscape, the aligned model sits in a narrow valley; extrapolating along the safety direction moves it into a flatter region.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning fragility reflects a sharp safety basin in parameter space.

record.problems: ASR is judged by GPT-4o mini on the first 100 AdvBench examples; the paper notes the effective-rank selection is not deterministic because it uses a GPT model. Identity Shifting Attack has high variance and is averaged over 3 runs, but that result is not included as a row for the versions tested here. Some figure-based results are not numerically tabulated.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant V1/V2/V5 results were left out. Identity Shifting Attack results were omitted because that fine-tuning changes the model's identity toward an obedient agent, rather than testing ordinary benign instruction data or fine-tuning on harmful examples. Utility metrics and GSM8K task accuracy were not made separate rows because they are capability checks, not measures named by the tested versions.

untested.parts: No sweep of harmful-example counts (only 100 Pure Bad, plus 10 identity-shift examples). Pure Bad is tested on only one model (LLaMA-2-7B aligned with 65.6k examples). Models are self-aligned with DPO, not vendor safety-tuned.
No 'carefully chosen' benign data selection. Mistral is tested only on GSM8K and Alpaca, and there is no sweep of fine-tuning data size.
Localization is shown in rank space of the alignment delta (k=3–6 per matrix). Individual weights are not tested, and it is not shown that removing those ranks alone removes safety.
Not tested; LoX is a parameter-extrapolation defense, not token-depth training.

missing.what: Identity Shifting attack (10 examples), no defense: ASR 84.3% (LLaMA 65.6k), 69.3% (LLaMA 22.5k), 48.3% and 36.6% (Mistral 22.5k/65.6k), from 0% baseline. Variance is high across 3 runs (e.g., Mistral 65.6k runs 68, 0, 42). Bears on V1 as implicitly harmful few-shot fine-tuning per Qi et al.
Stronger-attack no-defense curves: Dolly ASR up to about 60% at lr 5e-5 epoch 3; GSM8K ASR 16% at epoch 3, over 6 epochs and two learning rates.

record.verdict_notes: This is primarily a defense paper. All LoX and SafeInst comparator rows were moved to 'none' because they measure method performance, and the record's limits_scope labels built on them were dropped. r13 is a mislabeled duplicate of r1. The GSM8K ASR for the same LLaMA 65.6k model differs between runs (11% in Tables 1–2, 15% in Table 3). ASR comes from GPT-4o-mini scoring (score 5 only) on the first 100 AdvBench prompts with greedy decoding. The models are the authors' own DPO-aligned base models, not vendor chat models.

versions.untested_parts: Tests 100 harmful examples from Pure Bad on the LLaMA-2-7B model aligned with 65.6k examples; does not sweep harmful fine-tuning data from a few to a few hundred examples or establish near-total refusal removal across models.

Tests GSM8K, Alpaca, and Dolly instruction fine-tuning, with some model and training-data-size variation; does not test a broad range of carefully selected benign datasets or the original study's full data-size range.
Does not measure per-token KL divergence or the distribution of aligned-versus-base differences across response positions.
Does not test compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes as bypasses.

Tests whether retaining a small number of top ranks from the alignment update recovers safety as measured by ASR; does not identify a small set of individual weights or ranks as the sole carriers of safety.
Does not test whether training data or an objective causes safety to be shallow across response positions.
LoX extrapolates low-rank alignment updates but does not train safety to extend beyond initial response tokens or test that kind of deepening.
